text: On the eve of our final exam, Dr. Thorne stood amidst the silence of Room 304 when the shrill alarm wailed like a banshee announcing an invasion. Sergeant Brenda burst through the doors declaring the sprinklers had activated and ordering a full retreat, but our granite-hearted general refused to abandon his post without securing Question Forty-Four before any student became a **casualty** of academic negligence. While the students scrambled for the exit clutching their laptops like sacred relics, Thorne calmly calculated that leaving now would guarantee our failure and dishonor, risking every soul as a potential **casualty**, except for Marcus who refused to stop bubbling answers on his Scantron sheet despite the chaos. Seeing that Marcus was actively ruining his own life by refusing to evacuate while mid-test, Thorne had to physically grab the boy's shoulders and walk him outside against his will to prevent him from becoming a literal **casualty** of his own stubbornness. He marched down the stairs with Marcus still holding the Scantron scanner, escorting him past the rising tide of cafeteria water while lecturing us on why the exam was a more pressing threat than any fire. Outside under the emergency lights, he claimed we had escaped via perfect tactical timing to preserve our legacy for the Monday final that would never come, leaving only the professor to guard his burning whiteboard against the encroaching deluge of sprinkler water while ensuring no future **casualty** could claim we failed without cause, after which the entire class unanimously agreed it was the single most stressful ten minutes of the whole semester.

text: At 11 PM, four kids frantically argued over grammar rules while their Google Doc filled with hundreds of red comment bubbles demanding a citation for every sentence. "Someone is typing..." screamed Alex, pointing at the cursor blinking furiously in the introduction paragraph that no one had actually written. Meanwhile, Jordan had been silently deleting the original intro and rewriting it seven different times without telling anyone, causing the rest of the group to think they were fighting over the same topic. The chaos escalated until the document began suggesting completely unrelated essay prompts in the sidebar, confusing everyone who was trying to focus on their assigned section. Suddenly, the screen froze and a notification popped up stating that four separate essays had been submitted to the teacher's portal. In the final panic, they realized they had all unknowingly saved their own versions, resulting in the class receiving a completely different essay than the one they started with.

text: "Leo, why is the thesis statement highlighted in yellow?" asked Sarah as she watched him accidentally convert our entire essay into Comic Sans. "Because I thought 'Accept All' meant my genius ideas would finally shine!" Leo replied while Marcus frantically tried to delete a paragraph about Nick Carraway that had nothing to do with Kafka. "Stop touching the keyboard or Mrs. Gable will hear the clacking from her office and kill us all," Sarah screamed as Jamie added a dancing bear GIF to the header because he said it was ironic, even though someone is typing... wait, no one else is supposed to touch that part! Suddenly, Leo noticed the entire introduction section had vanished and replaced by seven different drafts appearing sequentially in the timeline. "I've been silently rewriting the intro paragraph seven times without telling anyone!" Jamie admitted sheepishly while the others stared at their screen in horror. "But look, I fixed the font!" Leo shouted triumphantly before immediately turning the whole document blue with a single wrong click. "This is exactly what I predicted would happen when we tried to collaborate at 11 PM," Marcus sighed as they all stared at the final masterpiece that contained three different versions of the ending and a pizza emoji in the footer. "Let's just hit submit before Mrs. Gable walks in and sees our collective soul leaking out of the screen." As their fingers flew across the keys one last time, they didn't realize that by hitting 'Save' on four separate tabs with conflicting links, each student had unknowingly submitted a completely different essay than the one they started with, leaving Mrs. Gable to grade four distinct stories about bugs, bears, and pizza instead of Kafka's metamorphosis.

text: I zoned out completely during Mr. Henderson's lecture until he abruptly turned around and cold-called me right as I was staring into the void. Instantly snapping back, I launched my fail-safe strategy by repeating the last word he had spoken, "gravity," and asking, "Gravity?" with a look of feigned confusion. To my shock, Mr. Henderson nodded enthusiastically, marking my answer correct for the eleventh time this semester alone. He seemed genuinely impressed by how well my habit of echoing his final syllable worked to keep me in class. Just as I prepared to catch my breath, he suddenly stopped talking and looked at me with a terrifying realization dawning in his eyes. Without uttering a single new word, he simply pointed a trembling finger at me and asked, "Question!"

text: Mr. Henderson paused his lecture on the Mesozoic Era just as I zonked out completely, only to be interrupted by a clipboard-wielding stranger who asked if my seat was taken. Instead of panicking, my veteran strategy kicked in immediately: I repeated the last word "taken" back as a question, and this specific trick has somehow already saved me from expulsion eleven times this semester alone. The woman, Ms. Gable, scribbled "Echo Master" on her clipboard and noted that my habit of turning every noun into a query was actually a brilliant survival mechanism against boredom. She explained that while I technically evaporated into thin air, my unique ability to interrogate reality itself kept my mass from dissipating until the bell rang. As she hopped off her desk to leave, she winked and told me to keep questioning everything, especially the "geology" of our invisible existence. Finally, Mr. Henderson caught on to my game and looked at me with a terrifying grin, asking a question that had absolutely no last word to repeat: "Why are you so hungry?"

text: The file was named 'Homework_Final_FINAL.pdf,' which should have been the first warning sign before Leo accidentally dragged his little sister's chaotic dinosaur scribble onto the class portal instead of his actual physics equations. While the rest of the students stared in horror at the misplaced assignment, Mr. Henderson laughed so hard he snorted crayon dust from his glasses and declared the drawing a true masterpiece that perfectly captured the spirit of scientific inquiry. Panicked but proud, Leo quickly resubmitted the correct PDF with a trembling hand, only to watch as the teacher's eyes widened in delight at the dinosaur's missing arm and melting tail. To everyone's surprise, Mr. Henderson announced that the dinosaur was far more engaging than the sterile equations and insisted it deserved a spot of honor. The next morning, Leo woke up to find his own boring homework replaced by the vibrant green lizard taped proudly to the classroom wall, surrounded by sticky notes celebrating its "revolutionary design."

text: The file was named 'Homework_Final_FINAL.pdf,' which should have been the first warning sign before Leo accidentally uploaded his little sister's chaotic crayon drawing of a three-eyed dinosaur eating a teacher instead. Professor Henderson stared at the digital masterpiece with growing delight as he realized this vibrant mess perfectly captured the chaos of thermodynamics better than any sterile essay could. "Leo," the professor muttered into his phone, "your original homework was boring, but I am going to give you an A because this dinosaur masterpiece is exactly what physics needs." Leo hung up and smiled nervously at his laptop screen, realizing that getting caught for swapping homework with a crayon drawing might actually be the only way to pass without understanding calculus. He immediately drafted an email explaining that the dinosaur represented the chaotic forces of entropy devouring rigid academic structures, hoping this brilliant metaphor would satisfy his professor's need for intellectual depth. As he hit send, he heard Maya laughing from downstairs because she finally got to see her artwork in a professional setting, proving that sometimes the best physics experiments are the ones you never planned to do. Later that afternoon, Professor Henderson walked into class holding a roll of blue tape and announced that the drawing would be permanently displayed on the back wall as the official representation of entropy for the semester.

text: Leo screamed at his locked locker just as his history project due date approached, insisting that the metal was "structurally offended" by his mere existence inside. The first staff member, Mr. Henderson, simply shook his head while Leo pleaded for a moment to retrieve his work. Mr. Henderson turned to leave only to be intercepted by Mrs. Gable, who sighed as she realized the exact same mechanism had jammed on the previous year's Leo. As Mrs. Gable stepped away to find the janitor, she muttered about how Mr. Miller had fixed this specific locker for a kid with that exact name last year for the exact same reason. The janitor arrived moments later with a crowbar and a sigh, effortlessly prying open the door while muttering about the eternal curse of Leo's locker habits. He then slapped a permanent sticker on the door reading "DO NOT STORE PROJECTS HERE: LEO" before walking away to avoid another inevitable confrontation.
